source.version: Undated manuscript retrieved from OSF; no version number printed in the PDF; full text with appended supplement.
source.title_on_document: Evaluating AI’s Ideas: The Role of Individual Creativity and Expertise in Human-AI Co-Creativity

supplement.holds: Supplemental Table 1: AI ideas and their AIDE ratings; Supplemental Table 2: descriptive statistics by problem; Supplemental Tables 3 and 4: alternative models using raw self-evaluation scores, with coefficients and standard errors; Supplemental Figure 1: correlation matrix.

paper_design_summary: One study recruited undergraduate engineering and psychology cohorts and used the same fixed sequence for everyone: generate an initial engineering solution, evaluate pre-generated AI solutions, then generate a second solution using the initial and AI ideas (pp. 12-15, Sections 3.1-3.2.2). Only the presentation order of problem topics was randomized; AI exposure was not allocated between conditions, and there was no control group (p. 15, Section 3.2.2; p. 33, Section 5.3). AIDE models scored originality and effectiveness of the generated solutions, and human coders classified the source of inspiration for second ideas (pp. 17-18, Section 3.3).

studies.label: Engineering design: initial ideas and revisions after AI suggestions

assignment.what_was_assigned: Everyone followed a fixed initial-idea, AI-evaluation, second-idea sequence. All participants saw the same pre-generated AI solutions; there were no separately assigned AI and no-AI groups. The between-person comparison used existing engineering and psychology student cohorts. The randomization described in the paper concerned presentation order of problem topics, not AI assistance or the order of AI and no-AI phases.
assignment.quote: Finally, using both their initial solution and the AI solutions, participants were instructed to generate their “most original and effective engineering solution” to the problem and self-evaluate their solution on its originality and effectiveness.
assignment.locator: p. 12, Section 3.1 (recruited cohorts); pp. 14-15, Section 3.2.2 (fixed sequence and randomized problem-topic order); p. 33, Section 5.3 (absence of a control group).

arms.name: Engineering students
arms.description: Existing cohort recruited from an introductory engineering design course; all completed the initial-idea and AI-exposed revision phases. This is an expertise cohort, not a randomized AI arm (p. 12, Section 3.1; pp. 14-15, Section 3.2.2).

arms.name: Psychology students
arms.description: Existing cohort recruited from the psychology subject pool; all completed the initial-idea and AI-exposed revision phases. This is an expertise cohort, not a randomized AI arm (p. 12, Section 3.1; pp. 14-15, Section 3.2.2).

participants.exclusions: 6 participants were excluded for failing to complete the entire study, leaving the reported retained sample of 311 people (99 engineering and 212 psychology students; p. 12, Section 3.1). Separately, 56 trials with an invalid response to either generated idea were excluded, leaving 1210 valid responses (p. 15, Section 3.2.2). The paper does not supply a revised unique-person count after trial filtering or reconcile the retained-person and trial totals; these are the printed counts.
participants.who: Pennsylvania State University undergraduates: 99 engineering students and 212 psychology students in the reported retained sample. The methods additionally exclude invalid trials but do not give a revised unique-person count after that exclusion.
participants.quote: Participants were recruited from the Pennsylvania State University (PSU) psychology subject pool and an introductory engineering course on engineering design as part of a larger study.
participants.locator: p. 12, Section 3.1 (retained sample counts); p. 15, Section 3.2.2 (subsequent trial-level exclusions).

ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated solutions through the OpenAI API before the study and selected six per problem, spanning high, moderate, and low AIDE-rated creativity. Participants evaluated the same supplied solutions and used them alongside their initial idea to produce a second solution; they did not chat with the model (pp. 14-16, Sections 3.2.2-3.2.3). The Water Access topic had five unique solutions because one was shown twice (p. 52, Supplemental Table 1 note).

task.description: Generate original and effective written engineering solutions for four problems: reducing city air pollution, increasing renewable energy use, helping people with memory impairments remember tasks, and improving remote access to clean water. For each problem, generate and self-rate an initial solution, evaluate the supplied AI solutions, then generate and self-rate a second solution (pp. 14-15, Table 1 and Section 3.2.2).
task.duration: Approximately 45 minutes for the entire study; task-specific duration not stated (p. 12, Section 3.1).

contrasts.reported: Idea 2 versus Idea 1: originality was higher, t(1209)=-7.04, p<.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank W=233232, p<.001. Z-scored AIDE means (SD), Idea 1 to Idea 2: engineering 0.371 (0.884) to 0.480 (0.897); psychology -0.255 (1.000) to -0.042 (0.635). The analysis unit is left null because the text says scores were averaged across the four problems, but the printed paired-test degrees of freedom are 1209 despite a reported retained sample of 311 people; the unit cannot be confirmed consistently from the manuscript.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Section 4.2 (paired t-test); p. 21, Table 3 and Section 4.2 (means, SDs, signed-rank test); p. 17, Section 3.3.1 (AIDE scoring); pp. 18-19, Sections 3.3.1 and 3.4 (stated averaging); p. 12, Section 3.1 (people count).

contrasts.reported: Idea 2 versus Idea 1: effectiveness was higher, t(1209)=-7.84, p<.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank W=248292, p<.001. Z-scored AIDE means (SD), Idea 1 to Idea 2: engineering 0.003 (0.975) to 0.247 (0.941); psychology -0.075 (0.938) to 0.127 (0.848). The analysis unit is left null because the text says scores were averaged across the four problems, but the printed paired-test degrees of freedom are 1209 despite a reported retained sample of 311 people; the unit cannot be confirmed consistently from the manuscript.
contrasts.locator: p. 20, Section 4.2 (paired t-test); p. 21, Table 3 and Section 4.2 (means, SDs, signed-rank test); p. 17, Section 3.3.1 (AIDE scoring); pp. 18-19, Sections 3.3.1 and 3.4 (stated averaging); p. 12, Section 3.1 (people count).

outcomes.name: Source of inspiration for the second idea
outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Engineering versus psychology cohorts: the distribution across six human-coded inspiration categories differed, χ²(5, N = 1210) = 28.60, p < .001. Completely New Idea: engineering 60 (15.5%) versus psychology 71 (8.6%); Direct Adoption of AI Idea: engineering 22 (5.6%) versus psychology 93 (11.3%). N counts coded responses, not people. Coding compares each second idea with that participant’s initial idea and the supplied AI ideas, rather than measuring diversity across people.
contrasts.locator: p. 18, Section 3.3.3 (human coding); p. 26, Table 6 (counts and percentages); p. 27, Section 4.5 (chi-square test).

eligibility.reason: AI exposure followed the same fixed before/after sequence for everyone, with no separately assigned control group; only problem-topic order was randomized (pp. 14-15, Section 3.2.2; p. 33, Section 5.3). This fails random assignment of AI assistance and is observational context. The reported retained sample is 311 people (p. 12, Section 3.1), and AIDE scores originality and effectiveness on the generated outputs (p. 17, Section 3.3.1).

one_line_finding: In a non-randomized before/after study of 311 students (p. 12), second ideas scored higher on originality, t(1209)=-7.04, and effectiveness, t(1209)=-7.84, both p<.001 (p. 20, Section 4.2), but the lack of a control group prevents separating practice effects from AI effects (p. 33, Section 5.3).
